To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) members of stereotyped racial groups are judged relative to group-based standards; 2) the tendency to shift academic standards for Black and White students when judging their competence is unrelated to other measures of prejudice; and 3) the tendency to use shifting standards predicts allocation of funds to Black student organizations, and this effect is moderated by implicit prejudice.

(a) the tendency to shift academic standards when judging the competence of Black and Whites is uncorrelated with self-reported prejudice, but (b) this tendency is correlated with race-relevant decisions, and (c) the tendency to use race-based shifting standards predicts the allocation of resources to Black student groups only among individuals with high levels of implicit prejudice.
the tendency to shift academic standards for Blacks relative to Whites is not correlated with other measures of racial prejudice but predicts reduced funding for a Black student organization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of stereotypes in the formation of attitudes and the role of attitudes in behavior.
the relationship between prejudice and the tendency to shift the standards by which one judges the competence of Blacks and Whites.
the question of whether the tendency to judge members of stereotyped racial groups relative to shifting standards is related to measures and correlates of racial prejudice and race-related behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the tendency for Whites to shift their academic competence standards for Blacks relative to Whites does predict race-relevant behavioral outcomes, but that the relationship is complex and is not well explained by measures of explicit prejudice or by implicit prejudice.
the shifting standards effect does indeed exist, and that it is related to implicit prejudice, which in turn relates to behavior.
there is no relationship between the tendency to shift and prejudice, but that the two may interact in some way to predict behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
shifting standards is a distinct form of prejudice that can be assessed independently from other forms of prejudice, but is not unrelated to the latter.
we found evidence of race-based shifting standards and that this effect was related to behavioral outcomes.

the tendency to shift the standards of evaluation for Black and White students when making academic evaluations is associated with reduced allocation of funds and other resources to Black students, but that this relationship is mediated by implicit prejudice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are different types of racism, some that may be more harmful than others.
shifting standards may not be a reliable marker of prejudice.
there are multiple forms of prejudice and that the tendency to shift subjective standards when judging members of stereotyped racial groups is one of those forms.
